## A Very Bad Start to 2009, With the Pain Set to Continue 



- In this issue are our initial estimates for the first quarter of 2009 and it doesn’t make pleasant reading. Trade data for Q1 is still only patchy but it is clear that wirerod and wire and cable volumes are well down across almost the whole world. We estimate that copper wire and cable consumption is 13.0% lower year-on-year and 1% down on Q4 2008. 



- All three of the developed world regions of North America, North East Asia and Europe have seen copper wirerod consumption fall by over 20% in Q1 compared to Q1 2008, whilst the Rest of the World has fared somewhat better with a 3.2% decline. The performance of the developing world has been boosted by China, where copper wirerod production is marginally up, and copper cable production is only slightly lower. 



- Early data for Q2 indicates that there is little sign of any upturn and most industry participants remain pessimistic about the outlook for this year. Some are taking comfort from the view that the bottom of the current cycle may now have been reached and that there could be a modest upturn in Q4. In our view the various stimulus packages around the world should begin to impact on wire and cable demand by Q4, but we are most likely looking at a potential double digit fall in the copper cable market this year.

© 2009 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 3 of 12 May 2009 Copper wire, cable and wirerod **www.crugroup.com** # Europe ### **A very difficult start to the year** We have made some revisions to our 2008 data, particularly for Eastern Europe, with new data showing that the important Russian and Polish markets were weaker than previously thought and that copper cable production in both these countries was hit more severely by the downturn than we had previously estimated. As a result we now believe that wirerod consumption in Eastern Europe fell by 3.6% compared to 2007, with copper cable production 4.0% lower. Our initial estimates for Q1 2009 show that the European market has continued to deteriorate with total copper wirerod production falling by 18.8% yearon-year, with consumption down by 22.5%. Compared to Q4 2008, rod consumption was down 6.7% with copper cable production down by 5.2%. Historically, since our data series began in 1998, Q1 has always been up on the previous Q4, so this indicates that the bottom of the current downturn may not yet have been reached. In Western Europe copper cable production was down by an estimated 19.8%, with the UK, Spain, Italy and Germany all seeing sharply lower output. The construction sector remains particularly weak in both Spain and the UK, with Germany also seeing a slowdown. The winding wire sector has been hardest hit with some countries seeing output down by as much as 40%. The German and Italian markets have been hit by falling exports, with the manufacturing sector in both these countries strongly reliant on this sector. The important German market is causing particular concern for 2009 as a whole with its economy now forecast to contract by 4.6% this year compared to a Eurozone average of 3.8%. After a very poor Q1, April continued the trend, but some of the people we have spoken to believe that there are signs just appearing that the bottom has now been reached and that there is the possibility of a very modest recovery in the months ahead, although this could easily be snuffed out by further bad news. ### **Russian demand looks very weak** After falling around 4% last year Russian copper cable production has plunged by around 40% year-onyear in Q1 of this year and the cable industry is very pessimistic about the prospects for the whole of 2009. Particularly badly hit have been the building wire, industrial and mining cable sectors. Industrial o

utput fell by 16% in January with inflation up 13.9% in February, in part due to the weakness of the rouble. Real GDP is forecast to contract by 3% in 2009, reflecting sharply lower commodity prices, on which the Russian economy is very reliant, along with restricted access to external financing and reduced external demand. The risk of a steep rouble devaluation remains the main threat to macroeconomic stability. Construction sector activity in Q1 was reportedly down by 60%, with machine building and the automotive sector also depressed. Since demand for electricity has fallen the utility sector is looking to cut back on investment which inevitably impacts on power cable production. Unlike in many other countries there is no sign of any significant government intervention that will directly boost cable demand. In addition to the fall in local copper rod demand, it is likely that exports will also be much lower this year, maybe falling by up to 50%, due to the change in cathode export duty as reported in the last issue of this Monitor. ever, with Encore’s Q1 sales volume down only 4% compared to Q1 and up 8.5% on Q4 2008. ### **Evidence from the end-use markets** Latest statistics suggest that the troubled US housing sector may be finally approaching stabilisation. In March, sales of new houses fell by 0.6% month-on-month to 365,000. Levels remain very low, although recent quantitative easing will bring down mortgage rates, supporting stabilisation. According to the Department of Commerce, home construction starts in March still plunged by 10.8% m-o-m and 54.1% y- o-y. Growth in non-residential spending is also slowing sharply, after helping support demand in 2008. Private non-residential spending was up just 1.7% y-o-y in March, whilst public non-residential spending was up 2.5% y-o-y. In Canada, data released by the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation showed that housing starts rose in March by 13.7% y-o-y. But the sector is still in difficulty due to the credit squeeze and lower incomes. North American new vehicle sales are expected to fall by 31% y-o-y in April, but rise by about 0.5% compared with March. Total new vehicle sales in February fell by 2.2%, with North American built passenger cars specifically down by 3.5%. In Mexico, vehicle production in February fell by 38.2% y-oy. For the first two months of the year output declined by 44.4% y-o-y, largely impacted by ailing demand from the US. Domestic demand for vehicles in the same period dropped by 29% y-o-y. ### **North American demand may have found a floor** After a Q1 that proved fairly steady compared to Q4 2008, market participants do not expect much of an improvement in any product segments in Q2, although few expect demand to get worse. Some are hoping things might be slightly better in the next quarter, with March and April proving better in many sectors than January and February. Overall, however, participants remain pessimistic. Lower demand for commercial wiring in particular is expected to have a negative impact on demand, whilst the residential market remains very poor. The automotive sector looks set to continue to see rationalisation, with Chrysler filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in April. Optimism about a recovery later in 2009 remains muted. tion ten years ago in Q1 1999. The latest data from the JCMA indicates that shipments were down 32.7% year-onyear in February and an estimated 25% in March. The winding and automotive wire sectors have been hardest hit with production down by over 30% in Q1, with appliance wire output also much lower. Continued investment by power utilities, exports and a reasonable level of construction activity means that the power cable sector is the best performer, with production down by less than 10%. In the face of current low levels of demand, the JCMA has issued a forecast for the next financial year ending in April 2010 which predicts that copper cable shipments will fall by 7.9%. This implies that for the calendar year of 2009 shipments will be slightly under 18% down, which is a little more optimistic than CRU’s forecast of around a 20% fall this year. In the face of such a fall, Furukawa Electric and Showa Electric are to merge their domestic electric wire sales operations, whilst leading appliance wire producer Onamba is to close two factories. The only real bright point is the HV power cable sector with the three main Japanese producers, J-Power, Viscas and Exsym, all reporting good export order books. ### **Taiwanese manufacturers really suffering** The Taiwanese cable industry continues to suffer with copper wirerod production down by 37.8% yearon-year in Q1 and copper wire and cable production 31.8% lower. Production of winding wire and electronic wire is only running at around half the level it was in Q1 2008, with power cable production down by almost a third in the first two months of the year. The government’s US$15bn stimulus package, of which a third is due to be spent this year, should start to have an impact later in the year, with a planned 10 major infrastructure projects boosting consumption of power cable. The leading cable manufacturers’ Q1 results reflect the impact of falling volumes and the lower copper price with most companies reporting revenues down between 40% and 50% year-on-year. For specialist winding wire manufacturer Jung Shing, turnover fell by 70%. ### **Korea faring slightly better than its neighbours** South Korea posted the worst performance out of the three North East Asian nations last year, but in Q1 copper wire and cable production was down by 12.8% year-on-year, which was better than both its neighbours, helped by good demand for utility power cables. The US$11bn stimulus package is aimed at among other things helping the real estate sector, plus boosting renewable energy production, which should help cable consumption. In the face of sluggish home demand, LS Cable, South Korea’s largest cable maker, is looking to boost export sales by 37% this year, with much of this likely to come from the HV power cable sector. © 2009 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 8 of 12 May 2009 Copper wire, cable and wirerod **www.crugroup.com** |North East A|sian co

strong demand for copper wirerod has been in Q1. Data on apparent refined copper consumption, which is one of the indicators we use for rod production, shows a jump of 37.9% for Q1 this year compared to the same period in 2008. However, imports of other forms of copper such as scrap were much lower and this, along with the fact that we believe that copper cathode is being stockpiled, means that true copper consumption growth is much lower. There are reports from some copper rod producers that demand has picked up towards the end of the first quarter and that they are now running at good capacity utilisations with healthy orders from the domestic market, but with so many producers it is hard to know if this is true across the whole industry. Also there are reports of copper rod being stock piled. 

Overall Chinese industrial production grew by 8.3% in March, compared to just 3.8% in February, but this is still well below the growth of around 15% typically seen in the first half of 2008. Construction completions remained quite low, with the area of buildings under construction rising, implying that project completions continue to be delayed. On the plus side vehicle production grew by 4.4% in the first quarter of this year compared to Q1 of 2008, power cable production was up and the combined production of washing machines, refrigerators, and freezers, grew by 6.3% on the same basis, driven by healthy local demand helped by subsidies for rural families. Large stocks of air conditioning equipment meant that production of this product fell by 23.4%. Electricity consumption fell by 4.3% in Q1, and this is normally a good indicator of industrial activity and implies that overall industrial production was down as a result of very low demand in export markets, as indicated by trade data. Thus overall we believe that Chinese wirerod consumption in Q1 fell by 0.7% year-on-year, but was up 7.7% compared to Q4 2008. 

### **Differing fortunes in the ASEAN region** 

Overall the ASEAN region is suffering a sharp fall in copper wire and cable production and consumption, but within the region the individual countries are experiencing differing fortunes. The two largest cable producers, Thailand and Malaysia, have seen sharply lower cable production as a result of the global economic crisis, particularly lower demand for electrical goods. Also Thailand’s political instability is not helping. Malaysia is one of the world’s leading winding wire producers, and this sector has been amongst the hardest hit in the current downturn. Another country where copper wirerod consumption is lower is the Philippines, with the large automotive harness business being badly hit by the slump in vehicle production in the US and Japan, the two main markets for its harnesses.

© 2009 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 11 of 12 May 2009 Copper wire, cable and wirerod **www.crugroup.com** # Industry News **Nexans** is to close its building wire plant in Germany. The plant at Vacha, which employs 160 people, has seen a sharp drop in demand due to the weak residential construction market in Germany and other European countries. This follows the closure of Nexans’ plant at Athlone in Ireland. The HV power cable sector is remaining strong and both **Ducab** and **NKT Cables** have announced new ventures. Ducab is to set up a new 30,000 cable tonnes plant in Dubai in partnership with ADWEA and DEWA. NKT Cables is establishing a new 51/49 jv with a Chinese partner to manufacture HV cables in China, which is due on stream at the end of 2009. Portuguese cable manufacturer **Cabelte** , is planning to set up a new jv in Libya to make fibre optic cables. The range will be extended to include power cables in a second phase. China’s **Jiangsu Jiangrun Copper Co. Ltd.** is targeting production of 240,000 tonnes of copper rod this year. The 320,000 tpy capacity plant began production in mid 2008, and produced 97,000 tonnes last year. Meanwhile **Tianjin Dawufeng Copper Semis Co. Ltd.** ’s second stage 150,000 tpy capacity rod mill is due on stream in May. This will double the company’s capacity. **Rea Magnet Wire** is to close a small speciality magnet wire unit at Fort Wayne in the US. Some assets will be sold to **Elektrisola,** the leading global producer of fine and ultra fine magnet wire, and the rest of the production will be consolidated into other units. **Belden** is to cut 110 jobs in Europe as part of a restructuring of its operations in the region. #### **Questions or comments may be addressed to:** **Rob Daniels:** +44 20 7903 2118 (robert.daniels@crugroup.com) This issue was completed on May 6 2009.
